prerequisites: Successful completion of the Mathematics examination
Successful completion of the General Physics examination

learning_outcomes.text: Students will acquire a thorough understanding of the fundamental principles of electromagnetism and electrical circuit theory. They will be able to understand the circuit model, the fundamental laws governing electrical networks, the behaviour of the main electrical components, and the methodologies for analysing circuits under DC, sinusoidal steady-state, and dynamic operating conditions. Furthermore, they will understand the role of electrical network theory as a general modelling framework for physical systems, recognizing its applicability across different engineering disciplines.

Students will be able to apply the acquired knowledge to analyse, solve, and synthesize simple electrical circuits by selecting the most appropriate modelling approach and analysis methodology. They will also be able to develop design solutions consistent with given specifications, critically evaluating their performance, complexity, and effectiveness.

Students will develop the ability to critically evaluate different circuit configurations, identifying the best compromise between simplicity, effectiveness, and design requirements. They will also be able to interpret the behaviour of electrical circuits based on the physical laws governing their operation.

Students will be able to communicate the fundamental principles of electrical engineering using appropriate technical language, correctly employ the terminology of the discipline, represent electrical circuits using standard electrical engineering methods and conventions, and rigorously discuss the analytical procedures adopted.

Students will develop a study approach based on the mathematical modelling of electrical systems and electrical network theory, acquiring competencies that can be transferred to advanced courses in electrical, energy, and automation engineering. They will also be able to identify analogies among physical systems belonging to different engineering fields by using electrical network theory as a general framework for analysis and modelling.

syllabus_topics: INTRODUCTION TO THE CIRCUIT MODEL Electric current intensity. Voltage and potential difference. Circuit model: bipoles, Kirchhoff's laws. Power and electrical energy, conventions. Main bipoles: resistor, capacitor, inductor, switch, open and short circuit, diodes, ideal and real voltage and current generators. Considerations on the characteristic of a bipole and on the maximum power supplied. Outline of application limits of the circuit model.

PROPERTY OF THE CIRCUIT MODEL - METHODS OF ANALYSIS – STEADY-STATE CIRCUITS Elements of graph theory. Eq. of Kirchhoff in matrix form, eq. of Kirchhoff linearly independent (dim). Canonical form of the equations. Methods of solution of the circuits through the node potentials and the mesh currents. Conservation of electric powers and Tellegen theorem (dim). Non-amplification properties for resistive circuits (dim). Properties of linear resistive circuits.

SINUSOIDAL CIRCUITS Sinusoidal circuits, phasors, symbolic or phasors method. Instantaneous and average powers in sinusoidal regime; complex, active, reactive, apparent powers and conservation properties. Boucherot theorem. Examples.

ANALYSIS AND SYNTHESIS OF DOUBLE BIPOLES Circuit elements with multiple terminals (N-poles), double bipoles. Double resistive bipoles and matrix representations (G, R, H and T). I, II and III form of reciprocity of the resistive d.b. (dim.). Controlled generators. Analysis and synthesis of double bipoles.

DYNAMIC CIRCUITS OF THE I AND II ORDER Dynamics of RC and RL circuits of the first order. Transient and permanent regime. Free and forced evolution. Dissipative circuits. Dynamics of second order circuits: RLC series. Continuity of state variables. Formulation with state equations. Associated resistive circuit method.
assessment_rules: The final examination consists of a compulsory written examination followed by a compulsory oral examination. Passing the written examination is required for admission to the oral examination and is valid only for the immediately following oral session. The final grade, expressed on a 30-point scale, is awarded after the oral examination and is not the arithmetic average of the two examinations, but rather based on overall performance. For attending students, two mid-term examinations are offered as an alternative to the final written examination; passing both admits students directly to the oral examination.
